title: The Nuclear Deal That Could Save NATO
gist: Ivo Daalder argues that Trump-era US conditionality has broken the 60-year NATO nuclear bargain, and that neither US-led NATO 3.0, national European arsenals, nor France's forward deterrence suffices. He proposes a renewed bargain with a European core led by France and the UK: modernized weapons, French entry into the Nuclear Planning Group, and doctrinal adjustments.

insights.claim: European governments have largely concluded that the United States is no longer a reliable ally; at a meeting this year, top foreign ministry officials from several European countries were asked who still believed the US would defend them, and not a single hand went up.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Collapse of confidence in Article 5 drives European defense spending and nuclear-posture decisions.

insights.claim: The current nuclear debate was triggered not by a shift in the global balance of power but by a unilateral change in US attitude toward Europe under Trump's second term, which has rejected a shared threat understanding and the indivisibility of members' security.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Policy-driven, not capability-driven, alliance stress is harder to reverse and more tied to US election cycles.

insights.claim: In August the Pentagon sent its 31 NATO allies a questionnaire stressing the conditionality of US commitment, asking them to profess loyalty to Trump's foreign policy, commit to buying US defense equipment and oppose 'buy European' initiatives.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Pressure for US-sourced procurement versus European preference is a direct driver for defense-contractor order flows on both sides of the Atlantic.

insights.claim: If Europeans doubt the US Article 5 commitment, US extended nuclear deterrence is effectively dead, because credibility to reassure allies matters more than credibility to deter adversaries.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Reassurance failure is the mechanism pushing allies toward proliferation.
insights.quote: If you don’t believe in the United States’ Article 5 commitment,” one of the officials attending the meeting told me, “then extended deterrence is effectively dead.

insights.claim: The Healey theorem holds that it takes only five percent credibility of American retaliation to deter an attack, but 95 percent credibility to reassure the allies.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: A reusable model: allied reassurance, not adversary deterrence, is the binding constraint on alliance nuclear policy.
insights.quote: It takes only a five percent credibility of American retaliation to deter an attack, but it takes a 95 percent credibility to reassure the allies.

insights.claim: The 1960s bargain had European states forgo nuclear weapons in exchange for a say in US nuclear policy through the NATO Nuclear Planning Group, and nonnuclear Europeans codified this in the 1968 Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty; about half a dozen European countries still host dual-capable aircraft able to carry US B-61 bombs.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: The NPT-linked architecture is what a European proliferation cascade would break.

insights.claim: Nuclear consultation and sharing arrangements proved far more important to reassuring allies than the hard-power measures US strategists favored, such as counterforce targeting, low-yield weapons and greater precision.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Argues political process matters more than weapon-system upgrades for alliance cohesion.

insights.claim: Washington's preferred NATO 3.0 option, with Europe leading conventional defense and the US keeping the nuclear umbrella, ignores the core problem because the administration has done nothing beyond assertion to convince allies of its commitment, and no extra deployments can offset conditionality.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: US offers to extend nuclear sharing to Poland and to develop a next-generation bomb will not restore trust on their own.

insights.claim: Some European leaders are openly considering national nuclear weapons: Polish PM Donald Tusk said in March 2025 'we would be safer if we had our own nuclear arsenal', Swedish politicians cite the 1960s secret program, and a Bundeswehr general said Germany 'needs its own tactical nuclear weapons'.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Nuclear-latency talk in allied capitals raises proliferation-cascade risk including in Asia.
insights.quote: we would be safer if we had our own nuclear arsenal, that is beyond doubt.

insights.claim: European nuclearization is unworkable because it would take years for Poland, Sweden or Germany to build deterrents, would break the NPT architecture and could spark an arms race that makes Europe less secure.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Argues national arsenals would take years and create a dangerous transition window.

insights.claim: France's March 2026 'forward deterrence' initiative, with nuclear training exercises and temporary forward deployment of nuclear-capable aircraft, has drawn ten European countries into bilateral nuclear steering groups, but Macron retained the 'four nos' including no joint decisions, no joint planning and no guarantee in the strict sense.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Real but limited French step; the retained limits cap how much it can substitute for the US umbrella.

insights.claim: France's doctrine of a warning shot followed by a devastating response offers fewer escalation options than NATO's flexible gradual-escalation strategy, which could make French nuclear threats less credible in a conflict over an ally.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Doctrinal narrowness is a credibility discount on a French-only umbrella.

insights.claim: The proposed solution is a renewed US-European nuclear bargain with a real European core led by France and the UK that bolsters both the European and US legs of deterrence, brings France into NATO nuclear consultation and extends nuclear sharing to more members, with the alternative being rapid proliferation.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Frames the policy path to watch: European nuclear burden-sharing inside NATO rather than outside it.

insights.claim: On hardware, the US should replace the B-61 gravity bomb with a stand-off missile reaching deep into Russia, and Europeans should fund a long-range nuclear-capable missile with a Franco-British warhead deployable on aircraft of nonnuclear allies, based in a wider range of NATO countries.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Implies multi-year European missile and dual-capable aircraft procurement if adopted.

insights.claim: France should join the Nuclear Planning Group without placing its forces under NATO command, and European NPG members could meet without the US in a caucus modeled on the existing meetings of countries hosting US nuclear forces.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Joining the NPG is the key signal of French willingness to integrate.

insights.claim: Implementation demands concessions from every party: Washington must accept it can no longer dictate NATO nuclear policy, Paris more NATO integration, London a second nuclear system and a joint warhead, and nonnuclear allies must finance missiles and reaffirm forgoing nuclear weapons.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Lists the political obstacles, so deal progress is slow and hard to price.

insights.claim: Russia has issued veiled nuclear threats against Europe repeatedly since 2022, most recently in September after NATO air exercises above northeastern Poland near Kaliningrad.
insights.speaker: Ivo H. Daalder
insights.so_what: Recurring nuclear signaling keeps European defense risk premia elevated.
